label: PolicyEngine household calculation, 2029-30
build: build fcfac709, policyengine-uk 2.177.7, certified in policyengine 6.20.2

runs.name: Health element and PIP removal (no replacement awards)
runs.description: The Universal Credit health element and PIP removed for under-25s, run together. Its two parts are each removal on its own.

runs.name: Higher Youth Allowance
runs.description: A separate run: under-25 claims with a housing costs element (the review's proxy for living independently) get the standard allowance for those aged 25 and over.

runs.name: Work allowance (illustrative)
runs.description: A separate, illustrative run: the report proposes a work allowance for young people in work but gives no amount; the amount here is our assumption, the current Universal Credit work allowance.

runs.name: Employer NI threshold
runs.description: A separate run: employers pay National Insurance from £10,000 a year, not £5,000, for 21 to 24-year-olds in retail and hospitality. The model passes the saving to pay.

assumptions: Renters pay £500 a month to a private landlord; the stored examples are in the North West.
A young person living with their parents is modelled as their own household with no rent: the parents' income and housing costs are not part of the calculation.
Council Tax and Council Tax Reduction are left out.
Benefit rates, the minimum wage and tax thresholds are the engine's for 2029-30, on the OBR forecast; every award is claimed in full, all year.
The report's replacement payments (such as its additional cost allowance) are not modelled, so nothing is paid in place of the health element or PIP.

Each run is compared with current law for the same household. The Youth Allowance, work allowance and employer National Insurance runs are separate: they are not added to the package or to each other.

Losing PIP daily living moves a single renter under 35 onto the shared accommodation rate of Local Housing Allowance, so the PIP part of a renter's change can include a fall in the Universal Credit housing element as well as the PIP itself.
A young person living with their parents holds no TV licence: the parents' household holds it.
Hours, wages (other than the employer National Insurance saving, which the model passes to pay) and housing costs are held fixed; no behavioural response is modelled.
